about.title: Ontario Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Ontario sits where three freeways meet, and much of the local workday happens in motion: on warehouse floors, in loading yards, and behind the wheel along I-10, SR-60, and I-15. When a shift ends with an injury instead of a paycheck, the questions come fast. Who pays for the emergency visit? Will hours get cut for reporting it? Is workers' compensation the only option? Under California law, workers' comp is usually your exclusive remedy against your employer, regardless of who was at fault. It is not always the whole story, though. If a subcontractor, a property owner, a defective piece of equipment, or another driver on Euclid Avenue caused your injury, a separate third-party claim may exist alongside the comp case. That claim carries its own two-year deadline. We are here to help Ontario workers understand which paths apply to your situation. Our team works on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.title: We look past workers' comp
items.desc: Comp is normally the only remedy against your employer, but a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or driver can open a separate injury claim. We review both tracks.

items.title: Deadlines get handled early
items.desc: California expects you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and third-party claims run on a two-year clock. An early review keeps both dates in view.

items.title: Free and contingency-based
items.desc: We charge nothing for a case review, and we only earn a fee if there is a recovery. Retaliation for reporting an injury is illegal, and we can address that too.

items.question: I was hit by another driver on the I-10 while making deliveries for my Ontario employer. Is that only a workers' comp case?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Because you were working, workers' comp likely covers your medical care and part of your lost wages. Since another driver may have been negligent, a separate third-party injury claim against that driver could also exist. That second claim must be filed within two years, so it helps to have us review it soon.

items.question: How quickly do I need to report a workplace injury in California?
items.answer: You should notify your employer within 30 days of the injury, ideally in writing. Reporting late can complicate your workers' comp benefits. If the injury developed gradually, tell your employer as soon as you connect it to your work.

items.question: Can my employer fire me or cut my hours for filing a claim?
items.answer: No. California law prohibits retaliation against workers who report an injury or file for workers' compensation. If you notice a sudden change in hours, duties, or treatment after reporting, let us know, because it may be part of your case.
